summary: Extends Kerberos, as defined in RFC 4120, so a client can send a list of the encryption types it supports in order of preference and the server can pick one that both sides support. This avoids guessing which encryption the other side can handle. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: You hand a shopkeeper a list of the languages you speak, best first. The shopkeeper picks the first one they also know, so you can both talk without guessing.

questions: how does kerberos pick an encryption type
how does kerberos pick a stronger encryption type
subtitle: Lets a Kerberos client and server agree on a stronger encryption type than the KDC picked for the ticket.

tldr.problem: The Kerberos KDC must pick the ticket session key encryption type from what it believes both sides support, so a stronger type that both sides understand cannot be negotiated.
tldr.mechanism: The client lists its encryption types in decreasing preference in the authenticator of the AP-REQ, and the server picks one and returns a matching subkey in the AP-REP.
tldr.outcome: Traffic after the exchange can be protected by a stronger cryptosystem than the one in the service ticket.

today: RFC 4537 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4120. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Ticket-Time Choices
sections.content:
In Kerberos as defined in RFC 4120, the Key Distribution Center (KDC) must limit the ticket session key encryption type (enctype) for a given server to one it believes both client and server support. If both understand a stronger enctype than the KDC chose, they cannot negotiate it.

As a result, protection of application traffic is often weaker than necessary, particularly when the server can support different sets of enctypes depending on the application software in use. RFC 4537 adds an extension so client and server can negotiate a different and possibly stronger cryptosystem for later communication.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket office picks a lock for you before it knows what locks you and the shop both have. This lets you and the shop pick a better lock yourselves.

sections.title: What the Client Sends
sections.content:
If the client prefers an enctype over the one in the service ticket, it SHOULD send a list of enctypes in decreasing preference order. The client picks from all enctypes available locally, based on local policy. It SHOULD NOT include enctypes less preferable than the ticket session key's enctype.

It also SHOULD NOT include negative (local-use) enctype numbers unless it knows in advance that the server uses the same negative numbers for the same enctypes.

If the ticket session key's enctype is in the list, it SHOULD be last. Otherwise that enctype MUST NOT be negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: You write your favorite choices first and never list ones worse than what you already have.

sections.title: The AD-ETYPE-NEGOTIATION Element
sections.content:
The list rides in the authorization-data of the authenticator inside the AP-REQ message. A new authorization data element type, AD-ETYPE-NEGOTIATION, is defined with the value 129.

The element is wrapped in an AD-IF-RELEVANT container, so a correctly implemented server that does not understand it ignores it. Its value is the DER encoding of an EtypeList, which is a SEQUENCE OF Int32 in decreasing preference order, favorite first.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is tucked into a part of the request that servers who do not care about it simply skip over.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
If the EtypeList is present and the server prefers an enctype from it over that of the AP-REQ authenticator subkey (if present) or the service ticket session key, the server MUST create a subkey using that enctype. It sends this negotiated subkey in the subkey field of the AP-REP message. The subkey is then used as the protocol key or base key for later communication.

The extension SHOULD NOT be used when the client does not expect a subkey in the AP-REP. The server MAY ignore the client's order, and how either side chooses is a local matter.
sections.plainLanguage: The shop picks the best choice from your list and tells you, and from then on you use that choice.

sections.title: Generating the Negotiated Subkey
sections.content: The KDC has a strong pseudo-random number generator, so the client can benefit from that randomness by reusing the KDC key data when generating keys. Implementations SHOULD use the service ticket session key value as a source of additional entropy when generating the negotiated subkey. If the AP-REQ authenticator subkey is present, it MAY also be used as a source of entropy.
sections.plainLanguage: When making the new secret, mix in some randomness from the ticket office, which is very good at being unpredictable.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The client's list and the server's reply enctype are part of encrypted data, so the security considerations are the same as for Kerberos encrypted data.

Both the list and the server's subkey are protected by the session key or sub-session key used for the AP-REQ. If a key for a stronger enctype is negotiated underneath a key for a weaker one, an attacker who can break the weaker enctype can also discover the stronger key. The benefit of the extension is that it minimizes the ciphertext under the weak enctype that an attacker can see.
sections.plainLanguage: The note listing your choices is itself locked with the old, weaker lock. The new lock helps for later messages, but cannot undo what the old lock exposed.

messages.label: AP-REQ
messages.note: Authenticator carries AD-ETYPE-NEGOTIATION with the EtypeList.

messages.label: AP-REP
messages.note: Subkey field holds the negotiated subkey.

data.title: EtypeList
data.code:
EtypeList ::= SEQUENCE OF Int32
    -- Specifies the enctypes supported by the client.
    -- This enctype list is in decreasing preference order
    -- (favorite choice first).
    -- Int32 is defined in [RFC4120].
